I went through Andrew Ng's *Agentic AI* course on DeepLearning.AI mainly because
I kept hearing "agentic" thrown around at work without a shared definition, and
I wanted a rigorous one before building anything else on top of Hermes Agent.
The course is good, but every example is generic, customer support bots,
research assistants. None of it touches what I actually do all day: segmenting
voids and lifted chips out of X-ray scans. So I rebuilt every example from
scratch, in my own domain, following the course's own five-module order. This
series is that rebuild, plus four more posts covering things the course does
not touch at all but that I think you need if you actually want to run this in
production.

If you read all nine posts and work through the code, you should be able to go
from zero to building, hardening, and shipping your own agent. That is the bar
I am holding myself to.

## What "agentic" actually means, cutting through the hype

A plain LLM call is one-shot: you send a prompt, you get text back, done. An
agentic system does three things a plain call does not. It acts, calling real
functions rather than just describing what it would do. It iterates, looking at
its own output and trying again if that is not good enough. It decides,
choosing what happens next, instead of you hard-coding every step.

Here is the distinction in my own terms. A plain LLM call can describe, in
prose, how you'd normalize a sixteen-bit X-ray TIFF. An agentic system actually
calls my `normalize_xray` function, looks at what came back, and decides
whether that result is good enough to hand to the next stage, or whether
something needs to be redone.

## The four design patterns

The course organizes everything around four patterns, and once you see them,
you start noticing them everywhere.

Reflection is an agent checking its own work and improving it, the automated
version of a code review. I use this to catch implausible segmentation masks
before a human ever sees them, more on that in [part two](02-reflection.qmd).

Tool Use is an agent calling real functions, code execution, database lookups,
APIs. This is the pattern I care most about, because it turns "a chatbot that
knows about segmentation" into "a system that actually runs my pipeline."
[Part three](03-tool-use-mcp.qmd) covers this in depth, including MCP, which is
how I now expose these same tools to Copilot and Cursor.

Planning is an agent breaking a task into sub-steps on its own, instead of me
writing that logic by hand every time.

Multi-Agent Collaboration is several specialized agents working together, a
preprocessing agent, a modeling agent, an error-analysis agent, instead of one
generalist agent trying to do everything badly.

## Jargon, explained simply

**LLM.** Large language model, the underlying engine, like GPT or Qwen, that
reads text and generates text back.

**Agent.** An LLM wrapped with the ability to call real functions and make
decisions about what to do next, rather than only producing text.

**Prompt.** The instructions and context you send to the model before it
responds.

**Design pattern.** A reusable way of structuring a solution to a common
problem, borrowed from regular software engineering, applied here to agent
behavior.

**Inference.** The act of running a trained model to get an output, as opposed
to training it.

## Setting up aisuite

The course builds everything on aisuite, a thin wrapper that gives you one
interface across multiple LLM providers. I like this choice for a practical
reason: model strings are written as provider, colon, model name, so switching
from a cloud model to my own local Qwen3 running on the GX10 is a one-line
change, not a rewrite. That matters a lot once you get into Reflection and Tool
Use, where the same agent code should work whether it's talking to GPT or to a
model sitting on your own GPU.

Install it with pip install aisuite, plus whatever provider extra you need.

Here's the minimal shape every example in this series builds from:

```python
import aisuite as ai

client = ai.Client()

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="openai:gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a semiconductor imaging QA assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "What does a bright blob in an X-ray void scan usually mean?"}
    ]
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

If you want to run this against a local model instead, you point the client at
an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, my own vLLM containers on port eight thousand
and eight thousand one work exactly this way, and nothing else in the code
changes.

## The domain, and why it's not a toy example

Every code example from here on touches a real problem I actually work on:
X-ray void detection in solder joints, AOI, or USM imaging. A few domain rules
I hold to throughout, because getting these wrong quietly wrecks your results.
Sixteen-bit TIFFs always get percentile-based normalization, never naive
min-max, since a handful of hot pixels will otherwise blow out your contrast.
Void regions appear bright, not dark, because lower material density means
higher X-ray transmission, the opposite of what most people expect walking in
from natural-image computer vision. And I never use elastic deformation as an
augmentation, because it distorts the exact void area I'm trying to measure.
